t.6.84.1: Thus the earth there became strewn and covered with monkeys whose limbs had been severed by those arrows of Daśagrīva.
t.6.84.2: They could not withstand that irresistible, blazing shower of Rāvaṇa's arrows coming from one side, just as moths cannot withstand a blazing fire.
t.6.84.3: Tormented by the sharp arrows, they fled in all directions, crying out, like elephants engulfed by tongues of fire and being burned alive.
t.6.84.4: In that battle Rāvaṇa advanced, scattering the ranks of the monkeys with his arrows, as the wind scatters great clouds.
t.6.84.5: Having swiftly wrought a slaughter of the forest-dwellers, the lord of the rākṣasas then hastened and approached Rāghava in battle.
t.6.84.6: Seeing those monkeys broken and fleeing in the battle, Sugrīva placed Suṣeṇa in charge of the troop and quickly set his mind on fighting.
t.6.84.7: Having entrusted that heroic monkey, his own equal, with his charge, Sugrīva, armed with a tree, set out to face the enemy.
t.6.84.8: At his sides and behind him, all the troop-leaders themselves followed, carrying great rocks and huge trees of various kinds.
t.6.84.9: The mighty Sugrīva, roaring in battle with a great voice, struck down many others of various kinds and slew the foremost rākṣasas.
t.6.84.10: And the huge-bodied lord of the monkeys crushed the rākṣasas, as the wind at the time of the end of the age crushes the towering trees.
t.6.84.11: Upon the ranks of the Rākṣasas he rained down a shower of rocks, just as a cloud rains a shower of hailstones upon flocks of birds in a forest.
t.6.84.12: Struck by those showers of rocks hurled by the king of the monkeys, the rākṣasas fell with their heads shattered, like mountains cut down.
t.6.84.13: Then, as the rākṣasas were being destroyed on every side, routed by Sugrīva, falling and crying out aloud,
t.6.84.14: The rākṣasa Virūpākṣa, an invincible bowman, proclaimed his own name, leapt down from his chariot, and mounted the shoulders of an elephant.
t.6.84.15: Mounting that elephant, the great chariot-warrior Virūpākṣa, roaring with a terrible din, rushed upon the monkeys.
t.6.84.16: At the head of the army he loosed terrible arrows upon Sugrīva, and, gladdening the rākṣasas who had been seized with fear, he made them stand firm.
t.6.84.17: That lord of the monkeys, deeply pierced by that rākṣasa with sharp arrows, became enraged, and, being of great wrath, set his mind upon slaying him.
t.6.84.18: Then the heroic monkey, uprooting a tree in the battle, rushed forward and struck down that great elephant right in front of him.
t.6.84.19: But that great elephant, struck by the blow from Sugrīva, drew back the distance of a bow's length, sank down, and roared.
t.6.84.20: But that mighty rākṣasa, swiftly leaping away from the crushed elephant, then turned to face his enemy and advanced against the monkey.
t.6.84.22: Then Sugrīva, greatly enraged at him, seized a huge rock resembling a rain-cloud and hurled it at Virūpākṣa.
t.6.84.21: Seizing a sword and a shield of bull's hide, he of swift prowess, as though menacing Sugrīva, advanced upon him as he stood firm.
t.6.84.23: Seeing that rock hurtling toward him, the bull among rākṣasas, exceedingly valiant, stepped aside and then struck with his sword.
t.6.84.24: Enraged, with that sword he struck down the armor of Sugrīva at the head of the army, and he, smitten by the sword, fell.
t.6.84.25: Rising up, the monkey who had fallen dealt him a blow with the palm of his hand, equal to a thunderbolt and making a terrible sound.
t.6.84.26: That demon skilfully evaded the slap raised against him by Sugrīva and struck him on the chest with his fist.
t.6.84.27: Then Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, seeing that his own blow had been evaded by that rākṣasa, became still more furious.
t.6.84.28: That monkey saw an opening in Virūpākṣa's defense, and then in fury he brought down a mighty slap upon his temple.
t.6.84.29: Struck by a slap of the palm like the thunderbolt of great Indra, he fell to the ground, drenched in gore and vomiting blood.
t.6.84.30: They saw Virūpākṣa, his eyes rolling in rage, drenched in frothy blood, made even more hideous-eyed than before.
t.6.84.31: The monkeys saw their enemy quivering, rolling over on his side, drenched in blood, and roaring piteously.
t.6.84.32: Thus engaged in battle, those two mighty oceans of forces, of the monkeys and of the rākṣasas, roared terribly, like two great oceans that have burst their shores.
t.6.84.33: Seeing the mighty Virūpanetra slain by the lord of the monkeys, the whole host of monkeys and rākṣasas became like the raging, flooded Gaṅgā.
